name: ラミちゃんの台所 (Rami-chan no Daidokoro (Rami-chan's Kitchen))

claims.text: Lunch dal bhat (rice, lentil soup, and vegetable/curry sides) is a traditional Nepalese staple that is often naturally vegetarian, though this specific restaurant's preparation and cross-contact practices were not confirmed.

name: シャンティ スープカリー（渋谷店） (Shanti Soup Curry (Shibuya))

claims.text: No confirmation found on whether soy sauce or other seasonings used are wheat-free; standard Japanese shoyu (which contains wheat) is likely used unless confirmed otherwise by staff.

Vegetable-forward curry options (e.g. taro, paprika, and other vegetables) exist alongside the signature chicken soup curry, and at least one review characterized the restaurant as offering 'a good choice for vegetarians and meat eaters.'

Venue is a shared space with independent tenants operating on different days; recent search results list current operators as CAFE AmaLie (Sat/Sun 12-17), アジア家庭料理・百福 (Mon/Tue/Wed 18:00-22:30, Asian home cooking), plus ノムカフェ (Sat), f-on (Sun/Mon/Tue/Thu/Fri), テルカフェ (Wed) — a different lineup than the 2019 macrobiotic-Wednesday kitchen the GF/vegan labels rely on.

Asian home cooking (アジア家庭料理・百福) is a Thai/ethnic-style operator; such cuisine standardly uses wheat-containing soy sauce, fish sauce (ナンプラー) and oyster sauce — an unmitigated gluten hazard and a hidden non-vegan (fish sauce/dashi) hazard on multiple days of the week.
百福 posted an October menu revision notice (メニュー改定のお知らせ), indicating the current menu differs from what earlier sources documented.

un-gluten.com (あんグル), the GF guide, itself publishes an article titled 'おしょうゆがグルテンフリーと言われても除去を続けるべき理由' — i.e. even celiac-aware Japanese guides warn that soy sauce is a hazard; a listing on such a guide does not certify the whole rotating venue as GF.
HappyCow now categorizes Shinjuku Dialogue as 'Tokyo Coffee & Tea' rather than a restaurant, and no celiac/GF safety reviews for the venue could be surfaced on FindMeGlutenFree or HappyCow.

Listed on a Tokyo gluten-free guide site, which states the venue's menu/sweets avoid gluten, dairy, white sugar, trans fats, GMO grains and food additives (attributed to its macrobiotic-style kitchen).

The Wednesday guest kitchen's dishes and desserts were reported to use no animal products (meat, fish, eggs, dairy, butter), no white sugar, no refined salt, no chemical seasonings, no preservatives, and no artificial coloring.

name: ソウルフードインディア 水道橋店 (Soul Food India Suidōbashi)

claims.text: No specific gluten cross-contamination statement was found; naan and other wheat items are prepared in the same kitchen and tandoor as curries.
No specific vegan cross-contact statement found; curries and naan may be finished with ghee, butter, or yogurt-based dough unless requested otherwise.
A vegetable curry (ベジタブルカレー, mild) is offered as a standing option on both the lunch and dinner menus, served with naan or rice.

name: 讃岐うどん大使 水道橋麺通団 (Suidobashi Mentsudan (Sanuki Udon Ambassador)

claims.text: The shop's signature broth is iriko dashi, made from dried sardines/anchovies — a fish-based stock used throughout the menu, not a vegan option.

name: タカマル鮮魚店 本館 (Takamaru Sengyoten Honkan)

claims.text: Standard Japanese soy sauce (shoyu) typically contains wheat; no confirmation was found that Takamaru Sengyoten offers a wheat-free soy sauce alternative for sashimi/sushi service.

The restaurant's core dishes are simply prepared sashimi and sushi cuts of whole fish purchased directly from Tsukiji, which as raw, unseasoned cuts are inherently free of wheat/gluten before any sauce is added.

name: 天ぷら 新宿つな八 総本店（総本店別館） (Tempura Shinjuku Tsunahachi Sohonten (curren)

claims.text: No gluten-free protocol, alternative batter, or dedicated fryer is advertised anywhere; tempura is fried in shared oil used for the full menu, so cross-contact with wheat batter is expected on every item.
The tentsuyu dipping sauce central to the meal is made with standard (wheat-containing) soy sauce and bonito dashi; no wheat-free soy sauce alternative was found in any source.

Vegetable tempura, if ordered, would still be fried in oil shared with shrimp, fish, and eel, and the tentsuyu sauce is dashi-based (bonito), so a fully plant-based meal free of animal cross-contact is not achievable here.
Restaurant information indicates all tempura items are fried in the same shared oil, so full removal of allergens (including gluten) cannot be guaranteed even with advance notice.

As with most traditional Edo-mae tempura restaurants, the tentsuyu dipping sauce is soy-sauce and dashi based; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat unless a specific wheat-free (tamari) alternative is used. No wheat-free soy sauce option was confirmed in available sources.
Because all tempura (seafood, meat, and vegetable) is fried in the same oil, vegetable tempura would not be separated from seafood items in the fryer.

Restaurant information suggests staff will try to accommodate dietary requests when informed at the time of reservation or on arrival, but note that complete allergen exclusion is difficult given the shared frying oil.
